questions.question: The gene pool refers to the sum total of genes in the reproductive _____ of a population.
questions.baby_explanation: Think of a big pot of seeds. The pot holds the seeds (gametes) that will make the next children.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> This refers to the sum total of genes in the reproductive gametes of a population. -> Final answer: gametes
questions.common_mistake: Writing 'zygotes'. The pool is made of gametes; zygotes come from it.

questions.question: The gene pool can be taken as a gametic pool from which samples are drawn at random to form the _____ of the next generation.
questions.baby_explanation: You scoop two seeds from the pot and join them. The joined seed is the first cell of a new baby, called a zygote.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> It can be taken as a gametic pool from which samples are drawn at random to form the zygotes of the next generation. -> Final answer: zygotes
questions.common_mistake: Writing 'gametes' again. Gametes are in the pool; zygotes are formed from it.

questions.question: Gene or allele frequencies are the proportions of the different _____ of a gene being considered in a population.
questions.baby_explanation: A gene can come in different versions. Allele frequency just counts how common each version is.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Gene or allele frequencies are the proportions of the different alleles of a gene being considered in a population. -> Final answer: alleles
questions.common_mistake: Mixing it up with genotype frequency, which counts pairs.

questions.question: Genotypic frequencies are the proportions of the different _____ in the population resulting from the various combinations of these alleles.
questions.baby_explanation: Alleles are single letters. Genotypes are the two-letter words they make, like MM or MN. This counts the words.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Genotypic frequencies are the proportions of the different genotypes in the population resulting from the various combinations of these alleles. -> Final answer: genotypes
questions.common_mistake: Writing 'alleles'. Alleles are the letters, genotypes are the pairs.

questions.question: Freq of a allele = Number of a allele / Total number of _____
questions.baby_explanation: How many of my kind, divided by how many of everything.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Freq of a allele -> Final answer: alleles
questions.common_mistake: Dividing by the number of individuals instead of the number of alleles.

questions.question: Since the homozygotes have _____ of a given allele and heterozygotes have only _____.
questions.baby_explanation: A homozygote has two matching copies. A heterozygote has one of each letter, so only one copy of a given letter.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Since the homozygotes have two of a given allele and heterozygotes have only one -> Final answer: two, one

questions.question: The total number of alleles is _____ the number of individuals (each individual carries two alleles).
questions.baby_explanation: Everybody carries a pair, so 10 people means 20 alleles.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> the total number of alleles is twice the number of individuals -> Final answer: twice
questions.common_mistake: Using the number of individuals as the total.

questions.question: MN blood types are controlled by the _____ M and N alleles.
questions.baby_explanation: Neither letter hides the other. Both show up in MN people.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> (controlled by the codominant M and N alleles) -> Final answer: codominant

questions.question: Allelic frequencies can be calculated as the frequency of homozygotes, plus _____ the frequency of heterozygotes.
questions.baby_explanation: A heterozygote only gives one copy out of two, so we count half.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> allelic frequencies can be calculated as the frequency of homozygotes, plus half the frequency of heterozygotes -> Final answer: half

questions.question: Counting alleles and using genotypic frequencies are algebraically _____ and thus give identical results.
questions.baby_explanation: Two roads, same town. Both methods give exactly the same answer.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> these two methods (counting alleles and using genotypic frequencies) are algebraically identical and thus give identical results -> Final answer: identical
questions.common_mistake: Thinking one method is more accurate than the other.

questions.question: G. H. Hardy was a British _____ and W. Weinberg was a German _____.
questions.baby_explanation: One was a number person from Britain, the other a doctor from Germany. They found the same rule without meeting.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> G. H. Hardy, a British mathematician, and W.Weinberg, a German physician -> Final answer: mathematician, physician

questions.question: Hardy and Weinberg demonstrated the _____ of gene and genotype frequencies.
questions.baby_explanation: Constancy means staying the same.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> They demonstrated the constancy of gene and genotype frequencies. -> Final answer: constancy

questions.question: In _____ G.H Hardy and W. Weinberg resolved the paradox.
questions.baby_explanation: A year to remember: nineteen oh eight.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> In 1908 G.H Hardy and W. Weinberg, the paradox was resolved. -> Final answer: 1908

questions.question: Brachydactily is a _____ trait in humans characterized mostly by abnormally short thick fingers.
questions.baby_explanation: It is a dominant trait but still rare. That puzzled scientists.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Brachydactily for example, is a dominant trait in humans characterized mostly by abnormally short thick fingers. -> Final answer: dominant

questions.question: The Hardy-Weinberg rule relates allelic and genotypic frequencies in a population of _____, sexually reproducing individuals.
questions.baby_explanation: Diploid means two copies of every gene, one from each parent.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> a population of diploid, sexually reproducing individuals -> Final answer: diploid

questions.question: Aspect 1: The allelic frequencies at an autosomal locus in a population will not _____ from one generation to the next.
questions.baby_explanation: The share of each allele stays the same.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The allelic frequencies at an autosomal locus in a population will not change from one generation to the next -> Final answer: change

questions.question: Aspect 2: The genotypic frequencies of the population are determined in a predictable way by the _____ frequencies.
questions.baby_explanation: If you know the allele shares, you can predict the pair shares.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The genotypic frequencies of the population are determined in a predictable way by the allelic frequencies -> Final answer: allelic

questions.question: Aspect 3: If the equilibrium is perturbed, it will be reestablished within _____ generation of random mating.
questions.baby_explanation: One round of random mating is enough to reset it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> if it is perturbed, it will be reestablished within one generation of random mating at the new allelic frequencies -> Final answer: one

questions.question: Random mating means the probability that two genotypes will mate is the _____ of the frequencies (or probabilities) of the genotypes in the population.
questions.baby_explanation: Chance of both things happening is one chance times the other.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> the probability that two genotypes will mate is the product of the frequencies (or probabilities) of the genotypes in the population -> Final answer: product
questions.common_mistake: Adding the probabilities instead of multiplying.

questions.question: If individuals with similar phenotypes are mating more often than at random, _____ assortative mating is in force.
questions.baby_explanation: Like marries like.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> If individuals with similar phenotypes are mating more often than at random, positive assortative mating is in force -> Final answer: positive

questions.question: Matings between individuals with dissimilar phenotypes more often than at random is negative assortative mating, or _____ mating.
questions.baby_explanation: Opposites attract. Dis-assortative.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> negative assortative mating, or disassortative mating, is at work -> Final answer: disassortative

questions.question: _____ is the mating of related individuals, and _____ is the mating of genetically unrelated individuals.
questions.baby_explanation: In means inside the family. Out means outsiders.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Inbreeding is the mating of related individuals, and outbreeding is the mating of genetically unrelated individuals. -> Final answer: inbreeding, outbreeding

questions.question: Deviations from random mating alter _____ frequencies but not _____ frequencies.
questions.baby_explanation: Rearranging who marries whom changes the pairs, not the letters.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> deviations from random mating alter genotypic frequencies but not allelic frequencies -> Final answer: genotypic, allelic

questions.question: When populations are small or when alleles are rare, changes in allelic frequencies take place due to chance alone. These changes are called random genetic _____.
questions.baby_explanation: In a small group, luck can push things around.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> These changes are referred to as random genetic drift, or just genetic drift. -> Final answer: drift

questions.question: Mutation and migration cause the loss or _____ of alleles in the population.
questions.baby_explanation: Alleles can leave or arrive.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Allelic and genotypic frequencies may change through the loss or addition of alleles -> Final answer: addition

questions.question: The final assumption is that no _____ is occurring.
questions.baby_explanation: Nobody has an advantage for having a certain genotype.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> In other words, no natural selection is occurring. -> Final answer: natural selection

questions.question: The new Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is at the _____ allelic frequencies; it does not 'return' to previous allelic values.
questions.baby_explanation: It settles wherever the alleles now are. It does not go back.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The new equilibrium will be, however, at the new allelic frequencies -> Final answer: new

questions.question: After one generation of random mating, the three genotypes AA, Aa and aa have the frequencies of _____, _____ and _____ respectively.
questions.baby_explanation: AA is p times p. aa is q times q. The mixed pair can be made two ways, so 2pq.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> After one generation of random mating, the three genotypes, AA, Aa, and aa, have the frequencies of p2, 2pq, and q2, respectively. -> Final answer: p^2, 2pq, q^2

questions.question: In a chi-square test, we compare an _____ number with an expected number.
questions.baby_explanation: What we saw, against what we expected.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> In a chi-square test, we compare an observed number with an expected number. -> Final answer: observed

questions.question: The critical chi-square for one degree of freedom at the 0.05 level is _____.
questions.baby_explanation: The line in the sand. Stay under it and the population fits.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> the critical chi-square for one degree of freedom at the 0.05 level is 3.841 -> Final answer: 3.841

questions.question: The number of degrees of freedom must equal the number of phenotypes minus the number of _____.
questions.baby_explanation: Three phenotypes, two alleles: 3 minus 2.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> the number of degrees of freedom must equal the number of phenotypes minus the number of alleles -> Final answer: alleles

questions.question: PKU is expressed only in the _____ recessive state.
questions.baby_explanation: You need two copies of the recessive letter to show it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> which is expressed only in the homozygous recessive state -> Final answer: homozygous

questions.question: Only one child in _____ live births has PKU.
questions.baby_explanation: Very rare. One in ten thousand.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> only one child in ten thousand live births has PKU -> Final answer: 10000

questions.question: A recessive gene causing a trait as rare as one in ten thousand is carried in the heterozygous state by one individual in _____ (give the number).
questions.baby_explanation: Rare to show, but about one person in fifty quietly carries it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> is carried in the heterozygous state by one individual in fifty -> Final answer: 50

questions.question: A gene pool is defined as all of the _____ available among the reproductive members of a population from which gametes can be drawn.
questions.baby_explanation: Everyone's letters, thrown into one pot.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> A gene pool is defined as all of the alleles available among the reproductive members of a population from which gametes can be drawn. -> Final answer: alleles

questions.question: When genotypes of the two parents are different, the product is doubled to account for the matings being _____.
questions.baby_explanation: Mother MN with father NN is one mating. Mother NN with father MN is another. So count twice.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> when genotypes of the two parents are different, the product is doubled to account for the matings being reciprocal -> Final answer: reciprocal

questions.question: Six different mating types are possible, nine of them if the _____ are considered.
questions.baby_explanation: Counting who is the mother and who is the father.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Six different mating types relative to genotype combinations are possible, nine of them if the sexes are considered. -> Final answer: sexes

questions.question: Allele frequency and genotypic frequency mean the same thing.
questions.baby_explanation: Allele frequency counts single letters. Genotypic frequency counts pairs of letters.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Allele frequencies are the proportions of the different alleles. Genotypic frequencies are the proportions of the different genotypes. -> Final answer: False
questions.common_mistake: Using the two terms as if they were the same.

questions.question: What is the gene pool?

options.A: All the genes in the gametes of a population
options.B: The genes in one individual only

questions.baby_explanation: It is the big pot of everyone's seeds.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The gene pool is the sum total of genes in the reproductive gametes of a population. -> Final answer: A
questions.common_mistake: Thinking it belongs to one person.

questions.question: How many alleles of a gene does one diploid person carry?
questions.baby_explanation: One from mum, one from dad.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Each individual carries two alleles. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: A heterozygote Aa adds how many copies of allele A when counting alleles?
questions.baby_explanation: Aa has one big A and one small a.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Heterozygotes have only one of a given allele. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: For a gene with two alleles, p + q = 1.
questions.baby_explanation: The two shares make a whole.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> p + q = 1 and q = 1 - p -> Final answer: True
questions.common_mistake: Forgetting this and finding q separately.

questions.question: Who independently discovered the rule relating allelic and genotypic frequencies?

options.B: Hardy, a British mathematician, and Weinberg, a German physician

questions.baby_explanation: Two people, two countries, one rule.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> G. H. Hardy, a British mathematician, and W. Weinberg, a German physician, independently discovered the rule. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: Hardy and Weinberg resolved which problem?

options.A: Why dominant traits like brachydactily stayed at very low frequency

questions.baby_explanation: People thought dominant traits should take over, but they did not. They explained why.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Dominant traits such as brachydactily remained at low frequency. In 1908 Hardy and Weinberg showed gene pool is conserved from one generation to another. -> Final answer: A

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an assumption of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
questions.baby_explanation: The rule works only when nobody has an advantage.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The final assumption is that no natural selection is occurring. -> Final answer: C

questions.question: In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium the genotype frequencies AA, Aa, aa are:
questions.baby_explanation: Squares at the edges, 2pq in the middle.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(AA)=p^2, f(Aa)=2pq, f(aa)=q^2 -> Final answer: B

questions.question: Natural selection must be absent for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium to hold exactly.
questions.baby_explanation: If some genotypes survive better, the shares change.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> No individual has a reproductive advantage because of its genotype. -> Final answer: True

questions.question: Non-random mating changes allele frequencies.
questions.baby_explanation: It only reshuffles who pairs with whom. The letters stay the same.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Deviations from random mating alter genotypic frequencies but not allelic frequencies. -> Final answer: False

questions.question: Random genetic drift is most important in:
questions.baby_explanation: Luck matters more in a small group.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> When populations are small or alleles are rare, allelic frequencies change due to chance alone: genetic drift. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: The mating of cousins is an example of:
questions.baby_explanation: Cousins are in the same family.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Inbreeding is the mating of related individuals, e.g. cousins. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: Individuals with similar phenotypes mating more often than at random is:
questions.baby_explanation: Like marries like.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Similar phenotypes mating more often than at random: positive assortative mating. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: After a disturbance, equilibrium is re-established within one generation of random mating.
questions.baby_explanation: One round of random mating fixes it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> If it is perturbed, it will be reestablished within one generation of random mating. -> Final answer: True

questions.question: After a disturbance, the new equilibrium is at:
questions.baby_explanation: It does not go back. It settles where the alleles now are.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The equilibrium will be at the new allelic frequencies. -> Final answer: B
questions.common_mistake: Thinking it returns to the old values.

questions.question: Mutation and migration can add or remove alleles from a population.
questions.baby_explanation: New letters can appear or arrive, or leave.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Frequencies may change through the loss or addition of alleles through mutation or migration. -> Final answer: True
questions.common_mistake: Thinking they do not affect allele frequencies.

questions.question: The MN population starts with 0.30 MM, 0.40 MN, 0.30 NN. After one generation of random mating the genotype frequencies are:
questions.baby_explanation: p = q = 0.5, so the pairs are 0.25, 0.5, 0.25.
questions.common_mistake: Thinking genotype frequencies must stay the same.

questions.question: When the two parents have different genotypes, the mating frequency is doubled.
questions.baby_explanation: Either one can be the mum, so there are two ways.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The product is doubled to account for the matings being reciprocal. -> Final answer: True

questions.question: How many different mating types are possible for genotype combinations (sexes ignored)?
questions.baby_explanation: MMxMM, MMxMN, MMxNN, MNxMN, MNxNN, NNxNN.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Six different mating types are possible, nine if the sexes are considered. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: In the chi-square test for Hardy-Weinberg we compare:
questions.baby_explanation: What we saw against what we expected.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> We compare an observed number with an expected number. -> Final answer: A

questions.question: The critical chi-square for 1 degree of freedom at the 0.05 level is:
questions.baby_explanation: Remember three-eight-four-one.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The critical chi-square for one degree of freedom at the 0.05 level is 3.841. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: If the calculated chi-square (0.348) is less than the critical value (3.841), the population does not deviate from Hardy-Weinberg proportions.
questions.baby_explanation: Under the line means it fits.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Calculated chi-square is less than critical chi-square. -> Final answer: True

questions.question: For a Hardy-Weinberg test with 3 phenotypes and 2 alleles, the degrees of freedom are:
questions.baby_explanation: 3 minus 2.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> d.f. = phenotypes - alleles -> Substitution -> 3 - 2 = 1 -> Final answer: B

questions.question: PKU is expressed only in which state?
questions.baby_explanation: Two copies of the recessive letter.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> PKU is expressed only in the homozygous recessive state. -> Final answer: C

questions.question: A chi-square test can be used to verify Hardy-Weinberg proportions in the PKU example.
questions.baby_explanation: We started by assuming equilibrium, so we cannot test it. Also there are zero degrees of freedom.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Allelic frequencies were derived by assuming Hardy-Weinberg proportions. d.f. = 2 - 2 = 0. -> Final answer: False

questions.question: In a recessive disease, the frequency of affected people equals:
questions.baby_explanation: Two copies of the recessive letter: q times q.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(aa) = q^2 -> Final answer: C

questions.question: The frequency of heterozygous carriers is:
questions.baby_explanation: Mixed pair.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(Aa) = 2pq -> Final answer: C

questions.question: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium holds exactly in all natural populations.
questions.baby_explanation: It is only approximated in nature.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is approximated in natural populations. -> Final answer: False
questions.common_mistake: Saying it is exact in nature.

questions.question: One reason Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is approximated in natural populations is:

options.B: The equilibrium is reestablished after only one generation of random mating

questions.baby_explanation: It bounces back fast.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The equilibrium is extremely resilient to change because it is usually reestablished after only one generation of random mating. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: In a population of 1000 people the genotypes are AA = 360, Aa = 480, aa = 160. Find the frequency of allele A.
questions.baby_explanation: Count every copy of the allele, then divide by the total number of alleles.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(A) = copies of A / total alleles; total alleles = 2 x N -> Substitution -> copies of A = 2(360) + 480 = 1200; total = 2(1000) = 2000 -> Final answer: f(A) = 1200/2000 = 0.6

questions.question: In a population of 100 people the genotypes are AA = 49, Aa = 42, aa = 9. Find the frequency of allele A.
questions.baby_explanation: Count every copy of the allele, then divide by the total number of alleles.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(A) = copies of A / total alleles; total alleles = 2 x N -> Substitution -> copies of A = 2(49) + 42 = 140; total = 2(100) = 200 -> Final answer: f(A) = 140/200 = 0.7

questions.question: In a population of 100 people the genotypes are AA = 30, Aa = 50, aa = 20. Find the frequency of allele a.
questions.baby_explanation: Count every copy of the allele, then divide by the total number of alleles.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(a) = copies of a / total alleles; total alleles = 2 x N -> Substitution -> copies of a = 2(20) + 50 = 90; total = 2(100) = 200 -> Final answer: f(a) = 90/200 = 0.45

questions.question: In a population of 200 people the genotypes are AA = 10, Aa = 80, aa = 110. Find the frequency of allele a.
questions.baby_explanation: Count every copy of the allele, then divide by the total number of alleles.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(a) = copies of a / total alleles; total alleles = 2 x N -> Substitution -> copies of a = 2(110) + 80 = 300; total = 2(200) = 400 -> Final answer: f(a) = 300/400 = 0.75

questions.question: Genotype frequencies are f(AA) = 0.5, f(Aa) = 0.3, f(aa) = 0.2. Find f(A).
questions.baby_explanation: Take the homozygotes, then add half the mixed ones.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(A) = f(AA) + (1/2) f(Aa) -> Substitution -> = 0.5 + (1/2)(0.3) -> Final answer: 0.65
questions.common_mistake: Adding all of f(Aa) instead of half.

questions.question: Genotype frequencies are f(AA) = 0.16, f(Aa) = 0.48, f(aa) = 0.36. Find f(a).
questions.baby_explanation: Take the homozygotes, then add half the mixed ones.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(a) = f(aa) + (1/2) f(Aa) -> Substitution -> = 0.36 + (1/2)(0.48) -> Final answer: 0.6
questions.common_mistake: Adding all of f(Aa) instead of half.

questions.question: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, p = 0.6. Find the frequency of genotype Aa.
questions.baby_explanation: Find q first, then use the squares and the middle term.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q = 1 - p; f(Aa) = 2pq -> Substitution -> q = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4; f(Aa) = 2(0.6)(0.4) -> Final answer: 0.48

questions.question: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, p = 0.3. Find the frequency of genotype aa.
questions.baby_explanation: Find q first, then use the squares and the middle term.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q = 1 - p; f(aa) = q^2 -> Substitution -> q = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7; f(aa) = (0.7)^2 -> Final answer: 0.49
questions.common_mistake: Using p or q instead of the square.

questions.question: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, p = 0.8. Find the frequency of genotype AA.
questions.baby_explanation: Find q first, then use the squares and the middle term.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q = 1 - p; f(AA) = p^2 -> Substitution -> q = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2; f(AA) = (0.8)^2 -> Final answer: 0.64
questions.common_mistake: Using p or q instead of the square.

questions.question: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, p = 0.7. Find the frequency of genotype Aa.
questions.baby_explanation: Find q first, then use the squares and the middle term.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q = 1 - p; f(Aa) = 2pq -> Substitution -> q = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3; f(Aa) = 2(0.7)(0.3) -> Final answer: 0.42

questions.question: A recessive trait occurs at a frequency of 0.0004 in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Find the allele frequency q.
questions.baby_explanation: Recessive people are q times q. Take the square root to find q.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q^2 = frequency of recessive; q = sqrt(q^2); p = 1 - q; carriers = 2pq; normal = p^2 -> Substitution -> q = sqrt(0.0004) = 0.02; p = 0.98; 2pq = 0.0392; p^2 = 0.9604 -> Final answer: 0.02
questions.common_mistake: Taking the recessive frequency as q instead of q^2.

questions.question: A recessive trait occurs at a frequency of 0.04 in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Find the allele frequency p.
questions.baby_explanation: Recessive people are q times q. Take the square root to find q.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q^2 = frequency of recessive; q = sqrt(q^2); p = 1 - q; carriers = 2pq; normal = p^2 -> Substitution -> q = sqrt(0.04) = 0.2; p = 0.8; 2pq = 0.32; p^2 = 0.64 -> Final answer: 0.8
questions.common_mistake: Taking the recessive frequency as q instead of q^2.

questions.question: A recessive trait occurs at a frequency of 0.0004 in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Find the frequency of heterozygous carriers (2pq).
questions.baby_explanation: Recessive people are q times q. Take the square root to find q.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q^2 = frequency of recessive; q = sqrt(q^2); p = 1 - q; carriers = 2pq; normal = p^2 -> Substitution -> q = sqrt(0.0004) = 0.02; p = 0.98; 2pq = 0.0392; p^2 = 0.9604 -> Final answer: 0.0392
questions.common_mistake: Taking the recessive frequency as q instead of q^2.

questions.question: A recessive trait occurs at a frequency of 0.0001 in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Find the frequency of normal homozygotes (p^2).
questions.baby_explanation: Recessive people are q times q. Take the square root to find q.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q^2 = frequency of recessive; q = sqrt(q^2); p = 1 - q; carriers = 2pq; normal = p^2 -> Substitution -> q = sqrt(0.0001) = 0.01; p = 0.99; 2pq = 0.0198; p^2 = 0.9801 -> Final answer: 0.9801
questions.common_mistake: Taking the recessive frequency as q instead of q^2.

questions.question: A recessive trait occurs at a frequency of 0.09 in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Find the frequency of heterozygous carriers (2pq).
questions.baby_explanation: Recessive people are q times q. Take the square root to find q.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q^2 = frequency of recessive; q = sqrt(q^2); p = 1 - q; carriers = 2pq; normal = p^2 -> Substitution -> q = sqrt(0.09) = 0.3; p = 0.7; 2pq = 0.42; p^2 = 0.49 -> Final answer: 0.42
questions.common_mistake: Taking the recessive frequency as q instead of q^2.

questions.question: In a sample of 500 persons p = 0.4 and the population is assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. How many Aa individuals do you expect?
questions.baby_explanation: Work out the share, then multiply by the number of people.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> expected number = 2pq x N -> Substitution -> q = 0.6; 2pq = 0.48; expected = 0.48 x 500 -> Final answer: 240
questions.common_mistake: Giving the proportion instead of the number.

questions.question: In a sample of 200 persons p = 0.7 and the population is assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. How many aa individuals do you expect?
questions.baby_explanation: Work out the share, then multiply by the number of people.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> expected number = q^2 x N -> Substitution -> q = 0.3; q^2 = 0.09; expected = 0.09 x 200 -> Final answer: 18
questions.common_mistake: Giving the proportion instead of the number.

questions.question: In a sample of 1000 persons p = 0.76 and the population is assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. How many AA individuals do you expect?
questions.baby_explanation: Work out the share, then multiply by the number of people.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> expected number = p^2 x N -> Substitution -> q = 0.24; p^2 = 0.5776; expected = 0.5776 x 1000 -> Final answer: 577.6
questions.common_mistake: Giving the proportion instead of the number.

questions.question: In a population f(MM) = 0.3 and f(NN) = 0.3. What is the frequency of the MM x NN mating under random mating?
questions.baby_explanation: Multiply the two shares. If the parents are different, double it.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Under random mating the mating frequency is the product of the genotype frequencies; double it when the parents differ -> Substitution -> (0.3 x 0.3) x 2 -> Final answer: 0.18
questions.common_mistake: Not doubling when the parents differ.

questions.question: A sample of 100 persons has AA = 40, Aa = 40, aa = 20. Calculate the chi-square value for the fit to Hardy-Weinberg proportions.
questions.baby_explanation: Work out what you expected, then see how far off each count is.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> p = (2 x first + middle) / 2N; expected = p^2 N, 2pq N, q^2 N; chi-square = sum of (O - E)^2 / E -> Substitution -> p = 0.6, q = 0.4; E = 36, 48, 16; contributions 0.444, 1.333, 1 -> Final answer: chi-square = 2.778 with d.f. = 1. Critical value 3.841, so it fits Hardy-Weinberg
questions.common_mistake: Using proportions instead of numbers, or dividing by O instead of E.

questions.question: A sample of 200 persons has MM = 114, MN = 76, NN = 10. What is p, the frequency of the first allele?
questions.baby_explanation: Count the copies of the first letter and divide by all the letters.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> p = (2 x first homozygotes + heterozygotes) / 2N -> Substitution -> p = (2(114) + 76) / 400 -> Final answer: 0.76

questions.question: Three phenotypes are observed for a locus with two alleles. How many degrees of freedom does the Hardy-Weinberg chi-square test have?
questions.baby_explanation: Three groups minus two letters.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> d.f. = number of phenotypes - number of alleles -> Substitution -> 3 - 2 -> Final answer: 1

questions.question: A population is at equilibrium with p = 0.5. What is the frequency of the heterozygote?
questions.baby_explanation: Half the folk are mixed when both letters are equally common.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> 2pq -> Substitution -> 2(0.5)(0.5) -> Final answer: 0.5

questions.question: Haemoglobin genotypes in a sample: AA = 2017, AS = 783, SS = 4. Find the frequency of the S allele.
questions.baby_explanation: Count the letter in every person, then divide by all the letters.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> Allele frequency = copies of the allele / sum of all alleles -> Substitution -> total alleles = 2(2804) = 5608; copies of S = 791 -> Final answer: 791/5608 = 0.141
questions.common_mistake: Dividing by the number of people instead of twice that number.

questions.question: Haemoglobin genotypes in a sample: AA = 300, AS = 100, SS = 50. Find the frequency of the A allele.
questions.baby_explanation: Count the letter in every person, then divide by all the letters.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> Allele frequency = copies of the allele / sum of all alleles -> Substitution -> total alleles = 2(450) = 900; copies of A = 700 -> Final answer: 700/900 = 0.778
questions.common_mistake: Dividing by the number of people instead of twice that number.

questions.question: A recessive disease affects 0.0001 of a population of 1000000 people in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. How many carriers (heterozygotes) do you expect?
questions.baby_explanation: Find the hidden carriers hiding in the big group.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q = sqrt(q^2); p = 1 - q; carriers = 2pq x N -> Substitution -> q = 0.01; p = 0.99; 2pq = 0.0198; carriers = 0.0198 x 1000000 -> Final answer: 19800
questions.common_mistake: Using q^2 as q, or forgetting to multiply by the population.

questions.question: In a population q^2 = 0.16 for a recessive trait. What is the frequency of the dominant phenotype (AA and Aa together)?
questions.baby_explanation: Everyone who is not recessive shows the dominant look.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> dominant phenotype = 1 - q^2 -> Substitution -> 1 - 0.16 -> Final answer: 0.84

questions.question: If p = 0.8 for a dominant allele A at equilibrium, what fraction of the population shows the dominant phenotype?
questions.baby_explanation: Add the AA people and the Aa people.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> p^2 + 2pq -> Substitution -> q = 0.2; 0.64 + 2(0.8)(0.2) = 0.64 + 0.32 -> Final answer: 0.96

questions.question: A trait caused by a dominant allele shows two phenotypes. With two alleles, how many degrees of freedom would the chi-square test have for Hardy-Weinberg?
questions.baby_explanation: Two groups minus two letters leaves nothing to test.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> d.f. = phenotypes - alleles -> Substitution -> 2 - 2 -> Final answer: 0

questions.question: A population is 0.20 MM, 0.60 MN, 0.20 NN. After one generation of random mating, what is the frequency of MN?
questions.baby_explanation: Find the letter shares first. Then use 2pq.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> p = f(MM) + (1/2) f(MN); MN = 2pq -> Substitution -> p = 0.20 + 0.30 = 0.50; q = 0.50; 2(0.5)(0.5) -> Final answer: 0.5

questions.question: A population is 0.50 MM, 0.20 MN, 0.30 NN. After one generation of random mating, what is the frequency of NN?
questions.baby_explanation: Letter share first, then square.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> q = f(NN) + (1/2) f(MN); NN = q^2 -> Substitution -> q = 0.30 + 0.10 = 0.40; 0.4^2 -> Final answer: 0.16

questions.question: If q = 0.1 at equilibrium, how many times more common are carriers than affected people (2pq divided by q^2)?
questions.baby_explanation: A few are sick, but many more carry it quietly.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> ratio = 2pq / q^2 -> Substitution -> p = 0.9; 2(0.9)(0.1) = 0.18; q^2 = 0.01; 0.18 / 0.01 -> Final answer: 18

questions.question: A population has genotype frequencies 0.36 AA, 0.48 Aa, 0.16 aa. Is it in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

options.D: No, because the heterozygote must be 0.5

questions.baby_explanation: Check if the pairs match the letters.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> p = f(AA) + (1/2) f(Aa) -> Substitution -> p = 0.36 + 0.24 = 0.60; q = 0.40; p^2 = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48, q^2 = 0.16 -> Final answer: A

questions.question: Which statement about non-random mating is correct?

options.A: It changes allele and genotype frequencies
options.B: It changes genotype frequencies but not allele frequencies
options.C: It changes allele frequencies but not genotype frequencies

questions.baby_explanation: Only the pairings change.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Genotypic, but not allelic, frequencies change under nonrandom mating. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: Why were the offspring MN genotype frequencies different from the parents in the 0.30/0.40/0.30 example?

options.A: The parents were not in equilibrium

questions.baby_explanation: They had not yet been through one round of random mating.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> The initial parental genotype frequencies were not in equilibrium; one generation of random mating places them into equilibrium. -> Final answer: A

questions.question: Why is it reasonable to assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for PKU even though there was selection against it?

options.B: Because it is so rare (one in ten thousand), selection has a negligible effect on allelic frequencies
options.D: Because the population is infinitely large

questions.baby_explanation: A very rare trait changes the overall allele share only a tiny bit.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> When a genotype is as rare as one in ten thousand, selection has a negligible effect on allelic frequencies. -> Final answer: B

questions.question: A calculated chi-square of 6.2 with 1 degree of freedom at the 0.05 level (critical 3.841) means:

options.B: The population deviates from Hardy-Weinberg proportions

questions.baby_explanation: Over the line means it does not fit.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> Calculated chi-square is greater than the critical value 3.841 -> Final answer: B

questions.question: The heterozygote frequency 2pq is the sum of two equal terms: pq from A-father and a-mother, and pq from a-father and A-mother.
questions.baby_explanation: Two ways to make a mixed pair.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(Aa) = (p x q) + (q x p) = 2pq -> Final answer: True

questions.question: In 1908 Hardy and Weinberg showed that the gene pool is conserved from one generation to another.
questions.baby_explanation: Alleles do not disappear or grow on their own.
questions.exam_solution: Definition -> They independently demonstrated that a conservation of gene pool takes place from one generation to another. -> Final answer: True

questions.question: In a sample, f(AA) = 0.672, f(AS) = 0.261, f(AC) = 0.058. What is f(A), counting the A allele only from these three genotypes?
questions.baby_explanation: Take AA fully, and half of each mixed pair holding an A.
questions.exam_solution: Formula -> f(A) = f(AA) + (1/2) f(AS) + (1/2) f(AC) -> Substitution -> 0.672 + 0.1305 + 0.029 -> Final answer: 0.8315, about 0.831
